options.correct: A set of metrics on either the new code or the whole codebase that, if breached, marks the PR as failing the gate
options.distractor_1: Whether the developer has manually marked the PR as ready for review using SonarQube's web UI before merging
options.distractor_2: Whether the PR's commit messages follow the SonarQube-mandated conventional commits format (feat/fix/chore prefixes)
options.distractor_3: Whether the PR has been reviewed by at least two SonarQube-certified reviewers within the configured time window, with quality recorded as a side effect of the human review

before.explanation: Quality Gates are SonarQube's pass/fail mechanism — metrics like 'no new critical bugs', 'duplication < 3%', 'new code coverage > 80%' are configured and checked on each scan. Distractor 1 invents a manual ready-for-review step. Distractor 2 invents a commit message convention requirement. Distractor 3 invents a SonarQube reviewer certification. The metric set is configurable per project, with sensible defaults for new vs all code.

before.question: Why does SonarQube focus on 'new code' metrics rather than whole-codebase metrics for Quality Gates?

options.correct: New-code metrics let teams improve incrementally without backfilling years of legacy debt before the gate ever passes
options.distractor_1: New code is the only code SonarQube can analyse because it can't index files older than 30 days
options.distractor_2: Whole-codebase metrics are slow to compute, while new-code metrics run in under one second regardless of repo size
options.distractor_3: SonarQube charges by line of new code analysed, so whole-codebase mode is disabled in the free tier by default

before.explanation: The new-code-only approach is what makes SonarQube adoptable in real codebases — old debt is grandfathered while the team enforces a higher bar on new changes. Distractor 1 fabricates a 30-day analysis horizon. Distractor 2 (whole-codebase too slow) isn't accurate — scans index incrementally. Distractor 3 invents a per-line pricing model. The new-code window is configurable (previous release, fixed date, etc.) but the principle of 'don't make it worse' is core.

before.question: An experienced pipeline owner is asked to redesign a CI/CD pipeline that takes 40 minutes and ships once a week. Which prioritisation reflects mature production thinking?

options.correct: Fast signal first (parallelise + shard tests) and tighten the deploy gate (smaller batches, automated rollback) — speed of feedback is the dominant lever
options.distractor_1: Maximise pipeline reliability by adding 3 retries to every stage and disabling flaky tests for the next quarter to stabilise the build
options.distractor_2: Migrate to the newest CI tooling first; tooling churn unlocks 10x improvements that incremental changes cannot match
options.distractor_3: Reduce scope: cut tests that have caught fewer than 5 bugs in the last year and rely on production monitoring for the rest

before.explanation: The owner's first job is to compress the feedback loop so commits-to-ship is short and reliable — that's where speed and risk both come down. Distractor 1 (retries + disable flakes) trades signal for green checkmarks; production gets worse. Distractor 2 (tooling churn) is the rookie answer — gains rarely come from the tool. Distractor 3 (cut tests) trades coverage for speed without understanding the cost; flaky-and-slow tests get fixed, not deleted. Mature owners prioritise *useful* fast signal.

before.question: Which lesson would a pipeline owner most likely take from running a CI/CD system through 18 months of production?

options.correct: Reduce batch size — large infrequent merges produce most incidents; small, frequent merges produce most boring uneventful deploys
options.distractor_1: Centralise everything — replace decentralised team pipelines with a single org-wide pipeline that all changes flow through for consistency
options.distractor_2: Add gates — every deploy should pass through at least 5 approval gates to ensure no change reaches production without sign-off
options.distractor_3: Move to a custom in-house CI system — third-party CI tools (GitHub Actions, GitLab) cannot meet the reliability needs of mature pipelines

before.explanation: Small batch size is the single most consistent lesson from pipeline operations — it shrinks the change surface, eases bisection on regression, and keeps reviewers honest. Distractor 1 (centralisation) often slows teams and adds blocking dependencies. Distractor 2 (more gates) trades velocity for false-precision; gates without signal become rubber-stamping. Distractor 3 (build your own CI) is the classic 'not invented here' trap — almost never the right answer.
